text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, weakened by pneumonia and pressed by political foes to give up power, celebrated his 66th birthday on Saturday quietly, in the soothing company of his close family and selected associates.

Itar-Tass news agency said the president, who is recovering after the illness in his Gorki-9 residence outside Moscow, had invited only two officials to his birthday dinner -- Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and chief of staff Anatoly Chubais.

Tass said Chernomyrdin, fresh from Swiss mountain resort of Davos where he took part in the World Economic Forum, went to the dinner straight from the airport with a "huge bouquet and a personal gift" for Yeltsin which he kept secret.

Yeltsin, whose heart problems, multiple bypass surgery in November and double pneumonia in January had kept him away from the Kremlin office since re-election last July, is now having a hard time proving that he is still fit to rule Russia.

Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov, who along with Orthodox Patriarch Alexii II congratulated Yeltsin earlier in the day, said that he had found the president physically weakened but alert, active and committed to returning to work

"The president looked like anyone who had undergone a complicated heart operation and pneumonia, who is not fully fit," Interfax news agency quoted mayor Yuri Luzhkov as saying after visiting Yeltsin in the Gorki-9 residence outside Moscow.
"But the president is quite active and, judging by the speed of his mind and the depth of his thought, he is the same president we all used to know," Luzhkov added.
On Sunday Yeltsin will hold talks outside Moscow with French President Jacques Chirac, the first Western leader to see him since he was taken to hospital with pneumonia on January 8.

Political opponents insist that despite this, Yeltsin's general state of health is inadequate to the tasks he is facing as the leader of the 150-million strong country. They want him to cede some of his sweeping powers or give them up altogether.
Yeltsin's bad health has become a routine theme in the campaigns of many Russian politicians.
Ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky sent his formal congratulations to Yeltsin promising his support and urging him to take tougher anti-western and nationalist line.
"All sorts of impudent ethnic minorities are raising their heads while Russians are being humiliated and discriminated against," Interfax quoted his letter to Yeltsin as saying.
"Any state or foreign politician is welcome now to lecture Russia on what policy it should pursue, who to trade with, what to sell and what to buy."
But hours later the maverick politician was shown on television mocking the Kremlin tradition of sick leaders clinging to power to the last.

"(Communist leader Vladimir) Lenin died at work, so did (Josef) Stalin and...(Leonid) Brezhnev," he told a meeting of supporters shown on NTV commercial television. "Yeltsin is dying but he holds on to his post."
Yeltsin himself on Friday rejected calls by political foes to amend the 1993 constitution to pass some of his powers to parliament and the government.
"The president cannot agree with such proposals," the Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing.
"In his opinion the constitution...has shown it can work, played and still plays an important stabilising role in society."
